content: This updated Cochrane Review focuses on the use of lamotrigine as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition, affecting approximately 0.5% to 1% of the population. Despite the availability of various antiseizure medications, around 30% of epilepsy cases remain resistant to treatment. Pharmacological interventions are the primary approach for managing epilepsy, and lamotrigine, a second-generation antiseizure medication, has been shown to reduce seizure frequency when used in combination with other antiseizure drugs. However, its use is associated with certain adverse effects. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and harms of adding lamotrigine to existing treatment regimens, compared to adding a placebo or no additional treatment, in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared add-on lamotrigine with add-on placebo or no add-on treatment in patients of any age. The primary outcome was a reduction in seizure frequency by 50% or more, while secondary outcomes included treatment withdrawal, adverse effects, cognitive effects, and quality of life. The search for relevant studies was conducted on October 3, 2022, using databases such as the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE, without language restrictions. A total of 14 studies involving 1,806 participants were included in the review. These studies consisted of five parallel-group trials, eight cross-over trials, and one parallel study with a responder-enriched design. Participants included 38 infants, 199 children, and 1,569 adults. The baseline phases of the studies ranged from 4 to 12 weeks, while treatment phases lasted between 8 and 36 weeks. The review found that lamotrigine, when compared to placebo, likely increases the probability of achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (risk ratio [RR] 1.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 2.23; moderate-certainty evidence). There was likely little or no difference in the risk of treatment withdrawal for any reason between the lamotrigine and placebo groups (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.37; moderate-certainty evidence). However, lamotrigine was associated with a higher likelihood of certain adverse effects compared to placebo. These included ataxia (RR 3.34, 99% CI 2.01 to 5.55; moderate-certainty evidence), dizziness (RR 1.76, 99% CI 1.28 to 2.43; moderate-certainty evidence), nausea (RR 1.81, 99% CI 1.22 to 2.68; moderate-certainty evidence), and diplopia (RR 3.79, 99% CI 2.15 to 6.68; moderate-certainty evidence). There was likely little or no difference in the risk of fatigue between the lamotrigine and placebo groups (RR 0.82, 99% CI 0.55 to 1.22; moderate-certainty evidence). The authors concluded that lamotrigine is likely effective as an add-on treatment for reducing seizure frequency in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, its use is probably associated with an increased risk of specific adverse effects, such as ataxia, dizziness, diplopia, and nausea. There was no significant difference in treatment withdrawal rates between the lamotrigine and placebo groups. The included trials were relatively short in duration and involved a limited number of participants, providing no evidence on the long-term effects of lamotrigine. Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of lamotrigine and to compare it with other add-on therapies.
